title: `pasta` and `conmon` processes are sometimes left in calling process' control group
body:
Software versions - Container host - Podman: 5.8.3 - conmon: 2.1.12 - pasta: commit `587980c` - systemd: 257.13 - Running rootless - Development machine - Podman: 5.8.3
I have a web service (herein called *deployer*) which invokes Podman (using Node.js' `child_process.spawnSync()`) to create, start and stop containers. The *deployer* service is managed as a systemd unit. Note that in control group paths, I've used */.../* as a shorthand for */sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-33.slice/user@33.service/*. **Problem:** When I attempt to stop or restart the *deployer* service, systemd hangs while waiting for all remaining processes in the control group */.../app.slice/deployer.service* to exit. This never happens, since the `conmon` and `pasta` processes created by Podman when *deployer* starts containers are left in the control group. *conmon* is not moved to its own *libpod-conmon-\.scope* control group as it usually is. After 60 seconds, systemd kills the `conmon` and `pasta` processes, killing the containers they support. With `--restart=always` set on the containers, they are restarted. That said, no `pasta` process is created when restarting them, making the containerised application inaccessible over the network. When running Podman in an SSH session, the `pasta` process lands in the control group */.../user.slice/podman-\.scope* and becomes a child of the system instance of systemd (PID 1). This allows the shell to exit without killing *pasta* or waiting for it to exit. That said, this transient control group is only supposed to live as long as the `podman` process does, but is kept alive by *pasta*. In some cases—I forget exactly which—the user instance of systemd complains in the journal about "left-over process[es]": ```txt Aug 11 02:20:15 systemd[993]: podman.service: Found left-over process 3323 (pasta) in control group while starting unit. Ignoring. Aug 11 02:20:15 systemd[993]: podman.service: Found left-over process 3927 (pasta) in control group while starting unit. Ignoring. Aug 11 02:20:15 systemd[993]: podman.service: Found left-over process 24491 (pasta) in control group while starting unit. Ignoring. Aug 11 02:20:20 systemd[993]: podman.service: Unit process 3323 (pasta) remains running after unit stopped. Aug 11 02:20:20 systemd[993]: podman.service: Unit process 3927 (pasta) remains running after unit stopped. Aug 11 02:20:20 systemd[993]: podman.service: Unit process 24491 (pasta) remains running after unit stopped. ``` **Possible fix:** Explicitly move any spawned support processes (e.g., `conmon`, `pasta`, `slirp4netns` perhaps) to a dedicated control group like *conmon* sometimes is; *libpod-support-\.scope* may be a more accurate name. --- I've tested several different methods of invoking Podman and recorded the parent processes and control groups of the spawned processes. I've left notes ("⚠️") wherever I think behaviour may not be correct. 1. Running Podman on development machine using remote system connection. > `podman` → SSH connection → `sshd-session` → `podman.socket` → `podman.service` → ...
Details ⚠️ ```sh podman run \ --connection=foo \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine sleep 1000 podman run \ --connection=foo \ --rm \ --tty \ --interactive \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/podman.service* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../user.slice/libpod-conmon-\.scope* | | `pasta` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/podman.service*
⚠️ Being daemonless, Podman's service unit should only live as long as the `podman` process. | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../user.slice/libpod-\.scope/container* |
1. Running Podman on the host via SSH session.
Details ⚠️ ```sh podman run \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine sleep 1000 podman run \ --rm \ --tty \ --interactive \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `sshd-session` → `zsh` | */.../user.slice/podman-\.scope* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (PID 1)
⚠️ All other methods cause this process to be parented by the user instance of systemd, not PID 1. | */.../user.slice/libpod-conmon-\.scope* | | `pasta` | `systemd` (PID 1)
⚠️ *See above.* | */.../user.slice/podman-\.scope*
⚠️ Being transient, Podman's scope unit should only live as long as the `podman` process. | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../user.slice/libpod-\.scope/container* |
1. Running Podman on the host from a user service (*deployer*).
Details ⚠️ ```sh podman run \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine sleep 1000 ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `node` | */.../app.slice/deployer.service* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service*
⚠️ This process prevents the *deployer* service from being restarted without killing containers. | | `pasta` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service*
⚠️ *See above.* | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../user.slice/libpod-\.scope/container* |
1. Running Podman with `--cgroup-parent` on the host from a user service (*deployer*). ⚠️ This option seems to have no effect, even with an explicit `--cgroups` option. Is the example below incorrect?
Details ⚠️ ```sh podman run \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ --cgroups=enabled \ --cgroup-parent=user.slice \ alpine sleep 1000 ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `node` | */.../app.slice/deployer.service* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service*
⚠️ This process prevents the *deployer* service from being restarted without killing containers. | | `pasta` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service*
⚠️ *See above.* | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../user.slice/libpod-\.scope/container* |
1. Running Podman via `systemd-run` on the host from a user service (*deployer*). This works but adds some complexity for the caller. *deployer* only requires this for calls to `podman start`, not other invocations of Podman.
Details ⚠️ ```sh systemd-run \ --user \ --scope \ --slice=user.slice \ --unit=podman.scope \ podman run \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ alpine sleep 1000 ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `node` | */.../user.slice/podman.scope* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../user.slice/podman.scope*
⚠️ This works, but differs from the intended control group for this process. | | `pasta` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../user.slice/podman.scope*
⚠️ *See above.* | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../user.slice/libpod-\.scope/container* |
1. Running Podman with option `--cgroups=split` on the host from a user service (*deployer*). ⚠️ This alters the control group hierarchy, but does not move support processes to a separate control group to that which the user service runs in. Each invocation of Podman creates a new "runtime" control group and moves the user service into it, eventually leading to an infinite stack of control groups, e.g., *...deployer.service/runtime/runtime/runtime/[...]/runtime*
Details ⚠️ ```sh podman run \ --rm \ --detach \ --publish=1234:1234 \ --cgroups=split \ alpine sleep 1000 ``` | Process | Parent process | Control group | |-|-|-| | `podman` | `node` | */.../app.slice/deployer.service* | | `conmon` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service/runtime*
⚠️ The parent control group is split, and this new "runtime" group is never removed. The user service is also moved to this new group and never moved back. | | `pasta` | `systemd` (user instance) | */.../app.slice/deployer.service/runtime*
⚠️ *See above.* | | `sleep`/`sh` | `conmon` | */.../app.slice/deployer.service/libpod-payload-\* |
The system states above were verified with these commands: - `pstree --compact-not --hide-threads --show-pids --long` - `pstree --compact-not --hide-threads --show-pids --long --show-parents ` - `systemctl --user status` - `systemctl --user status ` In summary: - Methods 1 and 2 probably should have the same result, but do not. - Methods 3 and 4 have the same result. - Method 5 has allowed me to work around this issue.

comments.body: /assign

The fix is minimal and targeted - if we simply removes the artificial barrier that was preventing conmon from being properly scoped when running under systemd. On a Linux system running under systemd, this would allow podman commands invoked from a user service to work correctly with restart/stop operations.

I took some time to work through the code and understand the issue.

I assumed you have the network mode pasta enabled. Could you verify this for one of the affected containers with:
```
podman inspect <container> --format '{{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}}'
```

Podman, conmon and pasta seem to have somewhat independent cgroup placement mechanisms.

pasta does not appear to have any explicit cgroup relocation, so it inherits Podman’s cgroup and remains there.

Podman moves itself to a user-systemd scope if it does not own its current cgroup. This explains why it moves when started outside the user systemd hierarchy, e.g. from an SSH session. The user-systemd cgroups are owned by the user, which maps to UID 0 inside Podman’s rootless user namespace.

conmon normally gets moved into a dedicated libpod-conmon-<ID>.scope. However, this move is skipped when Podman detects a local invocation under systemd:

```
RemoteURI() == "" && INVOCATION_ID != ""
```

This explains why conmon stays in deployer.service when Podman is invoked directly from that service, while it gets its own scope in the remote-connection case.

I am new to this codebase so I may have missed some things.

I checked some of the commits to understand the rationale behind the specific cgroup behaviour, but haven‘t finished this analysis yet. Till now it looks Like the implementations were driven independently from each other.

A possible Solution could be to unify the behaviour for systemd service managed podman by either moving all helper processes plus container to their own cgroup or leave them all under the systemd service‘ scope to share its lifecycle.

@devchris123 
I appreciate your thorough assessment. You are correct – there is no cgroup relocation in pasta, which is why I've included that in my second update. I checked the container utilizes pasta network type.
Your assessment aligns with what I discovered:
1. conmon – The RemoteURI() == "" && INVOCATION_ID != " " condition helps prevent scope generation when Podman is operating locally in systemd. This means the flaw here is that conmon remains attached to the cgroup of the service.
2. pasta – No cgroup relocation. It derives Podman's cgroup and does not leave it.
3. Podman – Moves itself into a user-systemd scope provided it does not govern the cgroup.

My solution is in line with your initial recommendation: shift all helper processes into their own cgroup.
- conmon: the INVOCATION_ID check has been taken away so that it invariably uses libpod-conmon-.scope.
- pasta: utilized cgroups relocation in libpod-pasta-.scope (retaining the current rootless netns approach).
This means that conmon and pasta will be able to endure service restarts and containers would keep working. 

As for the second suggestion (to have everything within systemd service scope), it implies that this service cannot be restarted, thereby stopping containers altogether.

@TanayJalan 
I agree, that leaving leaving everything under systemd scope would still lead to the behaviour the user experiences.

I'm just thinking, that changing this to relocating pasta and conmon by default is technically a breaking change. There could be use cases, where this behaviour is actually desired and relied on. We can assume something triggered the remote uri and invocation ID additions to branch this behaviour.

A more defensive solution would be for example introducing a configuration to have conmon's and pasta's cgroups relocated in any case, but leave the current behaviour as default. Something like --separate-cgroups (just thinking out loud here).  Downside is this makes the code more complex.

@devchris123 I get why you're worried about breaking changes. I think this is a bug fix, not a change in how things work:

1. The way things work now was never meant to happen. We added the INVOCATION_ID check so systemd could deal with cgroups. It had an unexpected result. This kept conmon in the services cgroup. This was not what people wanted. It just worked because most people didn't restart systemd services while containers were running.
2. Rootless netns pasta already works this way. The idea of moving pasta to its scope is already in vendor/go.podman.io/common/libnetwork/internal/rootlessnetns/netns_linux.go:203-246. We're just using the idea for per-container pasta.
3. The called "breaking change" is actually fixing a bug. If someone was depending on conmon/pasta being killed when the service restarts they were depending on a mistake. The right way is for these processes to keep running through service restarts, which --restart=always is supposed to do.
4. Adding a flag makes things more complicated for no reason. A --separate-cgroups flag would force users to know about and pick this behavior. Most users don't know that conmon/pasta stay, in the services cgroup until the containers stop.
Moving these processes to their own scopes by default, like rootless netns does, is the right fix.

The fix I'm working on moves conmon and pasta to their own scopes (libpod-conmon-<ID>.scope and libpod-pasta-<ID>.scope), so they're no longer in the service's cgroup and won't be killed on restart. This should resolve both the hanging restart and the SIGPIPE issue.

if you need a more specific control, couldn't you move the processes under `/runtime` to the target cgroup you'd like?

Using the `--cgroups=split` option, I would need to manually move three processes:

- Since the `node` process is mistakenly moved into the new control group (*/.../app.slice/deployer.service/runtime*), it would need to be moved back to the service unit's control group (*/.../app.slice/deployer.service*).
- The `conmon` and `pasta` processes would need to be moved from the new "runtime" control group to a new group dedicated to a particular container's support processes (e.g., */.../machine.slice/libpod-support-<CONTAINER_ID>.scope*).

Starting another container afterwards could also fail when Podman tries to create a new "runtime" control group, since the old "runtime" control group may still exist.

Manually moving processes between control groups also isn't right, though, and *systemd* expects to be the only party managing its unit control groups. Units with the `Delegate` property enabled are expected to manage their own subtrees, but Podman isn't a unit. The `systemd-run` workaround avoids manually moving processes around and effectively forces Podman to behave as I think it should by default.

For what it's worth, I think of Podman as a management program that is separate from its spawned processes. If Podman or its calling process crashes, containers should not be killed (or half-killed), just as an SSH connection being dropped shouldn't shut down the remote machine. Without passing explicit command-line options that change the default behaviour and regardless of Podman is spawned in the process and control group hierarchies, I think new container processes should always land in a predictable place in the those two hierarchies. Currently, there's a lot of variation in where these processes land between the six methods of invoking Podman listed in the original issue.

you can't move them back.  cgroup v2 does not allow processes in non-leaf cgroups, that is why `/runtime` is created and populated.

If you want a new cgroup to be created and all the processes moved there, just combine it with `systemd-run --scope --user -p Delegate=true`.

@mnrx @giuseppe 
Thanks for the continued feedback on #29582.

The fix in this branch (a4464f5933) specifically addresses the pasta process being left in the service's control group when running podman from a systemd user service. It moves per-container pasta processes into a dedicated libpod-pasta-<random>.scope (matching the existing pattern for rootless netns pasta), so they no longer prevent service restart/kill.

Regarding --cgroups=split: as you noted, this creates a new "runtime" control group that's never cleaned up, leading to an infinite stack of groups. The current fix takes a different approach—relocating only the pasta process to its own scope without altering the user service's cgroup hierarchy.

The conmon process handling is tracked separately; the current change focuses on pasta. You can test the fix with:
podman run --rm --detach --publish=1234:1234 alpine sleep 1000

then restart the systemd service and verify pasta is in its own scope

Looking forward to your testing feedback.

I am not sure though that is what we want to do by default.  Creating a scope has its cost and for most users it doesn't matter.  If you want full control, you've already the possibility using `--cgroups=split`

@giuseppe Thanks for the feedback. You're right that scope creation has overhead - but the issue is specifically about systemd user services where pasta processes prevent service restart/kill. The default behavior was never intended to leave pasta in the parent service's cgroup. For users not running under systemd user services, the impact is minimal. The --cgroups=split option remains available for those who need fine-grained control. This fix targets the specific regression for systemd user service users without adding overhead for everyone else.
how do you decide if the new scope must be created or not?

@giuseppe—Just saw your comment as I was about to post this comment. Replies below.

> you can't move them back. cgroup v2 does not allow processes in non-leaf cgroups

I forgot about that. The "runtime" control group makes more sense with that in mind.

> Creating a scope has its cost and for most users it doesn't matter.

> how do you decide if the new scope must be created or not?

Podman already creates two scopes in most cases:

- */.../user.slice/libpod-conmon-<CONTAINER_ID>.scope* for the `conmon` process.
- */.../user.slice/libpod-<CONTAINER_ID>.scope/container* for the containerised process.

Creation of the first of these is skipped, however, when Podman is invoked by a user service. Additionally, the `pasta` process is not moved to a specific control group at all, unlike the other processes. Changing these two behaviours is the right fix, IMO.

I don't think I need any particuarly special configuration of control groups, I just want Podman to be more predictable. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't think the current behaviour has been specifically chosen, but has evolved as Podman has. I could format the results of the testing in the original issue as a control group tree—that might make them easier to interpret.

> just combine it with `systemd-run --scope --user -p Delegate=true`.

I'm using `systemd-run` to run Podman itself, not my software. I assume Podman currently makes *systemd* API calls to configure control groups, in which case `Delegate` is not needed. I mentioned `Delegate` before just to illustrate the added hassle of managing control groups manually.

if we move pasta (or any other running process, like e.g. fuse-overlayfs) to the already created cgroup then that is correct to do.

I don't think we want to create yet another cgroup when running from a systemd service, just make sure the `INVOCATION_ID` environment variable is not set when running Podman.

> if we move pasta (or any other running process, like e.g. fuse-overlayfs)

Yeah—I'd suggest changing the name of the "libpod-conmon" control group to "libpod-support", and placing `pasta` and any other support processes in that group.

> I don't think we want to create yet another cgroup when running from a systemd service

Are you suggesting to only create the control group for the containerised process, and not the support group? What is the distinction between these two running modes? Is the current behaviour required to support running containers as *systemd* services? Even without invoking Podman from a user service, there is variation in behaviour. Each SSH session creates a *.scope* control group (via *systemd-logind*), for instance, but a local terminal creates */.../app.slice/vte-spawn-\<UUID\>.scope* (at least in GNOME Terminal). When Podman is used remotely with the `--connection` option, Podman runs in its own service and the `pasta` process ends up keeping `podman-<PID>.service` running indefinitely (see method 1 in the original issue).

I'd like to make Podman behave as consistently as possible across these different cases. If there's a specific reason to re-use the existing control group and specific criteria for this behaviour, then we can accommodate that. Is the reasoning purely control group overhead? If so, how would you feel about a hypothetical `--cgroups=always` option that skips the running-in-a-service check?

I'm happy to add some documentation to clarify some of this, too.

> Creation of the first of these is skipped, however, when Podman is invoked by a user service. Additionally, the `pasta` process is not moved to a specific control group at all, unlike the other processes. Changing these two behaviours is the right fix, IMO.

I think this is the point we disagree about.  If I run Podman from a systemd service I don't expect its process to escape to some other cgroup.

It is not clear what happens when Podman is the only process in the systemd service. Podman processes are moved somewhere else and the current service will just terminate because there are no more processes left?

Can't you just unset `INVOCATION_ID` from your service before exec'ing Podman?

> I think this is the point we disagree about. If I run Podman from a systemd service I don't expect its process to escape to some other cgroup.

Which process? The containerised process is currently left in a *libpod-<CONTAINER_ID>.scope/container* group, which is *outside* of the control group the user service is in (see method 3 in the original issue). The support processes are left in the service's control group.

Part of our disagreement may stem from me conceptualising containers as quasi-VMs rather than as processes. I don't think of a container as a conceptual "child" of the process that called Podman.

> It is not clear what happens when Podman is the only process in the systemd service.

*systemd* will not consider a service stopped until all processes exit. `systemctl stop ...` will block until this happens. If processes don't exit within ~90 seconds, they are terminated.

- Under method 1, the service in question is `podman-<PID>.service` (created by `podman.socket`). This service will live for as long as the `pasta` process does.
- When starting containers in a regular SSH session (method 2), the `pasta` process is left in `podman-<PID>.scope`.

Both of these "podman" control groups would normally be destroyed when Podman exits. When running `podman ps`, `podman pull`, etc., these groups are destroyed. Only when starting containers with networking are these long-lived `pasta` processes created and left behind. By contrast, the `conmon` process is moved elsewhere.

I would expect the `podman` process itself to sit in my user service's control group and be a child of the `node` process, but that `podman` process is only short lived.
